Jet
JET
verb (Gen X slang)
From jet, a forceful stream (Old French jeter, to throw; Latin iactare), which gave the 1940s jet engine and jet airliner; to jet, to travel fast, follows in mid-century American speech. In late-1980s and 1990s hip-hop and teen slang it became a casual word for leaving quickly: "I gotta jet," "Let’s jet." It is unrelated to jet, the black mineral (as in "jet-black"), which comes from Gagai in Asia Minor.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"I gotta jet" means I have to leave, and fast. The picture is a jet airliner — here one second, gone the next. Gen X loved speed in its words as in its music, and jet fit perfectly. The Christian observation is that Scripture has two things to say about haste, and they are both worth teaching a child. The first is a warning: "he that hasteth with his feet sinneth" (Pro 19:2). Hurry can be a vice — the rush that skips thinking, the dash out the door that leaves a chore undone and a mother unthanked. The second is a command: some things deserve all the speed we have. "I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments" (Psa 119:60). When Jesus looked up into the sycamore and said, "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house" (Luk 19:5), the little man jetted: "he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully" (Luk 19:6). Behind both lies a sober fact: our lives themselves are jetting by. "It is soon cut off, and we fly away" (Psa 90:10); "what is your life? It is even a vapour" (Jas 4:14). A father can laugh when his son says he has to jet, and then teach him the difference: don’t rush past people, don’t hurry into sin — but when Christ calls, come down quickly, and receive Him joyfully.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X slang (late 1980s–1990s, from the jet airliner) for leaving quickly; Scripture warns against sinful haste (Pro 19:2) and commends the haste of Zacchaeus coming down to Christ (Luk 19:6).

JET, v. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s) To leave, especially quickly. "I gotta jet — my mom’s waiting." "Let’s jet."

From the jet engine and jet airliner (1940s onward); earlier jet, a forceful spurt, from Old French jeter, to throw.

Companions: I’m outtie, Audi 5000, bounce, peace out. Unrelated to jet, the black mineral.

Webster 1828: JET, v.i. [See the Noun.] To shoot forward; to shoot out; to project; to jut; to intrude. 1. To strut; to throw or toss the body in haughtiness. 2. To jerk; to jolt; to be shaken. [This orthography is Rarely used. See Jut.]

Decode for parents: "I gotta jet" is just goodbye; teach the difference between hurrying past people and hastening to obey (Psa 119:60).

Key Scripture

Pro 19:2 — "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth."

Psa 119:60 — "I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments."

Luk 19:5 — "And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house."

Luk 19:6 — "And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully."

Jas 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Modern Corruption

Jet prizes the fast getaway; Scripture distinguishes the sinful haste that rushes past wisdom from the holy haste that runs to obey, and reminds us our whole life is flying away.

expand to see more

The hurried life. Gen X grew up with jet travel, fast food, and the remote control; its children have the instant message. Speed became a virtue in itself. But Proverbs pairs haste with ignorance: the soul without knowledge and the feet that hurry (Pro 19:2) belong together. A family always jetting from one thing to the next has no time to think, to pray, or to listen. The slower virtues — patience, attention, thanksgiving — are the first casualties of the rush.

Make haste, and come down. Yet Scripture has its own urgency. The Psalmist hurried to obey (Psa 119:60), and Zacchaeus scrambled down from the tree the moment Jesus called his name (Luk 19:5-6). Life is a vapour (Jas 4:14), and the call of Christ is not one to answer later. The Christian is meant to be slow to sin and quick to repent — to jet away from evil and jet toward the Savior.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin iactare (to throw) → Old French jeter → English jet (a forceful stream) → 1940s jet engine and airliner → Gen X jet (to leave fast); Scripture: make haste, and come down (Luk 19:5).
